Meeting: Compliance requirements review — PII access logging
Attendees: Renee (Legal/Compliance), Faiza (Eng), Ben (Support ops manager)

Renee: We're preparing for a customer's vendor security audit next quarter, and
one of their requirements is that we can produce an access log for any PII field
a support agent has viewed — who looked at what, when, and ideally why.

Ben: Today support agents can see full customer records — email, phone, billing
address, last four of payment method — with no logging of individual field views,
just a generic "ticket opened" log.

Faiza: So we'd need field-level access logging, not just record-level. That's a
bigger change than it sounds — right now the UI renders the whole customer object
in one API response, so we don't have a clean signal for "agent viewed the phone
number" versus "agent viewed the shipping address."

Renee: The audit requirement is specifically about PII fields — email, phone,
physical address, payment info. It doesn't need to cover every field in the
system, just those categories.

Faiza: That narrows it. We could tag those specific fields in the schema and log
access at the point they're serialized into an API response, rather than trying
to track UI-level rendering.

Ben: Would this slow down the support tooling? Agents already complain the
console is slow during peak ticket volume.

Faiza: Logging itself should be cheap if it's async — write the log entry after
the response is already on its way, not blocking on it. I don't expect a
noticeable slowdown, but we should measure it rather than assume.

Renee: Retention is the other piece. The audit wants at least 12 months of access
history, queryable by customer or by agent. What's our current log retention?

Faiza: Our general application logs roll off after 30 days. This would need its
own retention policy, separate from the default, and it needs to be tamper-evident
— an agent shouldn't be able to delete their own access record.

Ben: Do we need a "reason" field, or just record what was accessed? Some audit
frameworks want a stated business reason per access.

Renee: This particular auditor doesn't require a reason code, just who/what/when.
I'd rather not add a reason field now if it's not required — it adds friction for
agents and we can always add it later if a future audit needs it.

Faiza: Understood. Open question for me: does this apply retroactively, or only
to access going forward from when we ship it? I assume forward-only, but want
that confirmed since it affects how we message this internally.

Renee: Forward-only is fine, we'll note the start date in the audit response.
